 For many retirees living on a fixed income, rapid price increases (1) in the post-pandemic era have been hard to absorb. In fact, as inflation has surged, older generations have seen their spending growth lag behind other generations (2), and their discretionary spending has fallen below that of households overall. 
 This could soon change, though. As Bank of America (1) reported, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (3) already provided a temporary income boost for many retirees, as eligible seniors 65 and over can claim a new tax deduction of up to $6,000 per taxpayer through 2028. A lower tax bill means more money to spend on other things.

 Now, a coming Social Security change in 2027 could provide even more relief through a cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA. The COLA was announced in October and will take effect in January, resulting in a 3.6% benefit increase for all Social Security recipients. 
 COLAs happen most years, but some groups feel they aren't as effective as they should be at maintaining the buying power of Social Security. While COLAs are calculated using a consumer price index to try to ensure benefits keep pace with inflation, the Senior Citizens League believes the formula is flawed, and the real buying power of benefits has declined by almost 14% since 2016 (4). 
 But this year, the Bank of America Institute said that the recently announced 3.6% increase could actually provide a "meaningful boost" in 2027. Because the COLA is relatively high (tied for the fifth highest (5) since the 80s), if inflation ends up moderating as experts anticipate, the increase in benefits may actually outpace the growth in prices. 
 In other words, the 3.6% benefit bump may not just help seniors avoid losing ground. It could help them actually gain ground, increase their purchasing power, and potentially narrow their spending gap. 
 This should come as a welcome relief to older Americans, as if the prediction pans out, the extra wiggle room in their budget next year could allow them to make purchases they've been putting off. 
 Story Continues Of course, even a big Social Security raise doesn't mean Social Security is sufficient to cover every retiree's spending needs. Social Security is meant to work with savings to support seniors, so older Americans should invest wisely and have a solid financial plan for their later years.
